intro.title: The thinking behind the work.
intro.description: I build products, teams, and systems around the people using them. These stories show the decisions I made and what the work changed.
intro.closing: There is always a better way, together we can find it.

studies.title: One platform. Five properties.
studies.summary: I built a shared commerce platform with a part-time engineer. A fully branded property went from six weeks to launch to two.
studies.role: Product and design lead; front-end development.
studies.scope: Brand experience, platform roadmap, and the commerce funnel.
studies.collaboration: A part-time engineer built and maintained the platform with me; four experience designers covered the properties.
studies.source: docs/case-studies-sanitized.md: The Alternative to Five Sites Was Five Teams; docs/copy-register.md: Section A, DentalPlans; B26; B27

proof.label: of company revenue growth in one measured year

atAGlance: Every new storefront would repeat the same manual work.
A shared platform made brand identity and promotions configurable.
A fully branded commerce site went from six weeks to launch to two.

sections.label: The Problem
sections.title: The first site worked. Copying it would multiply the work.
paragraphs: The first version was a branded storefront on an off-the-shelf theme. Sale pricing and strikethrough values were typed in by hand, product by product, every time a promotion changed.
It answered a useful question: would people buy from a focused brand experience? They did. Leadership wanted more properties, and cloning the site would carry every manual task into every new one.

sections.label: The Journey
sections.title: I brought a roadmap for the work we could stop doing.
paragraphs: I argued for a platform and phased the work deliberately. A full rewrite would have been difficult to fund. Each release replaced a piece of manual labor with a capability the next property could reuse.

Brand configuration came into the content management layer. Theme tokens separated each storefront's identity from the application underneath it. Shared product and provider data meant engineering could add information once and every site would inherit it.
I owned the experience through marketing pages, cart, and checkout, along with the front-end build. The platform was built and maintained by me and a part-time offshore engineer.
sections.decision: Remove repeated work before adding the next storefront.

sections.label: The Solution
sections.title: One foundation, with room for each brand.
paragraphs: The platform combined token-based themes, a shared source for products and providers, scheduled multi-phase promotions, and one-button deployment per environment. A property could change its identity without changing the underlying application.

Source attribution connected the acquisition experience to the storefront. Promotion, copy, and messaging changed according to the visitor's source, down to specific affiliate identifiers. The page said what the ad promised.
points: Brand identity as configuration
Shared product, provider, location, and review data
Scheduled promotions across the commerce funnel
Deployment for one property or all of them

sections.label: The Results
sections.title: The business grew without rebuilding the machinery.
paragraphs: Launching a fully branded property fell from six weeks to two. Five properties ran on the platform.

In one measured year, finance credited the properties with 47% of company revenue growth, 27% of total lead capture, and 20% of overall revenue. The growth figure is a share of the company's growth increment in that year.
Four experience designers covered the properties. Automation absorbed repetitive updates, leaving people time for the decisions that changed the experience.
sections.takeaway: You create velocity by making the work smaller.

studies.title: Building an experience design practice
studies.summary: I built the research, systems, and measurement a new design function needed while we delivered a product integration.
studies.scope: Design foundations, research, measurement, executive facilitation
studies.collaboration: A small experience design function working across product, engineering, marketing, and leadership.
studies.source: docs/case-studies-sanitized.md: Building the Function That Was Not There; Making UX Visible in the Numbers; Four Executives, Four Different Customer Journeys; docs/copy-register.md: B37
atAGlance: Delivery started before a design practice existed.
Build reusable foundations alongside the integration work.
I put research, design systems, and measurement in place while the team delivered an integration.

sections.label: The Problem
sections.title: The delivery work arrived before the practice.
paragraphs: There was no prior experience design team, no design system, no research practice, and no measurement framework. The function had to take shape while shipping a major integration.
Spending all our capacity on screens would leave the next project with the same missing foundations. I needed to make room for the operating work inside the delivery work.

sections.label: The Journey
sections.title: Where the work repeated, I left something behind.
paragraphs: I built the token foundation before the page count grew. Usability testing came with a report format that could be reused. Executive workshops had a board system, moderator guide, and scenario matrix, so the next session could start with working materials.

Measurement needed its own structure. I paired experience metrics with business outcomes and drew on real user monitoring, moderated testing, and survey data. Each source answered a different question.
sections.decision: Treat the foundations as part of delivering the product.

sections.label: The Solution
sections.title: A practice another designer could use
paragraphs: The function gained documented tokens, a repeatable usability-testing report, a measurement framework, and materials for executive workshops.
The scorecard combined experience measures and business outcomes. The customer feedback program had a vendor recommendation and was ready for instrumentation.
points: Tokens and governance before more pages
Research with a repeatable report format
An experience scorecard tied to business outcomes
Workshop materials that outlive the meeting

sections.label: The Results
sections.title: The next project had a starting point
paragraphs: Subsequent work could use the documented tokens, research format, scorecard, and workshop materials. The customer feedback program was ready for instrumentation.

studies.title: Four executives, four different customer journeys.
studies.summary: I designed a working session that brought department leaders together around the same customer journey and its handoffs.
studies.collaboration: C-level participants across marketing, digital health, engineering, and commerce.
studies.source: docs/case-studies-sanitized.md: Four Executives, Four Different Customer Journeys
atAGlance: Each department held only part of the customer journey.
A custom working session followed concrete customer scenarios.
I brought the leaders responsible for each part of the experience into one working session to examine the handoffs.

sections.label: The Problem
sections.title: Customers had declined to organize themselves into departments.
paragraphs: A major integration crossed marketing, digital health, engineering, and commerce. Each leader held a piece of the customer journey. No shared view covered the path from first awareness through subscription and refill.
The gaps between those views were the places where the customer changed hands. We needed to examine the complete journey together.

sections.label: The Journey
sections.title: I designed the conversation before the session.
paragraphs: I built a custom board system for the integration. A generic template would have shaped the discussion around somebody else's problem.

I wrote a moderator guide and constructed a scenario matrix. The group would work through concrete customer situations, with enough structure that the session did not depend entirely on my improvisation.
sections.decision: Put the owners of both sides of a handoff in the same conversation.

sections.label: The Solution
sections.title: Follow the customer across departments
paragraphs: I used customer scenarios to walk the group through the journey. When a handoff failed, the people responsible for both sides were present to examine it. The moderator guide kept the discussion on the customer situation.
points: A board system built for the integration
A moderator guide for repeatable facilitation
A matrix of concrete customer scenarios

sections.label: The Results
sections.title: A shared journey and a record of the gaps
paragraphs: The group documented the end-to-end journey with executive participation. Handoff failures were discussed with their owners present. The boards, moderator guide, and scenario matrix remained available for future sessions.

studies.title: How customers look for products
studies.summary: I led navigation research with customers and used the findings to guide the category structure and shop-by paths.
studies.scope: Navigation, category structure, and shop-by paths
studies.collaboration: Research findings prepared for the team making navigation and information architecture decisions.
studies.source: docs/case-studies-sanitized.md: Navigation Decisions Were Being Made on Taste

proof.label: a stronger entry point into the catalog

atAGlance: Navigation choices depended on internal preference.
Moderated testing examined how people used the navigation.
I led research into how people looked for products and brought the findings into the navigation redesign.

sections.label: The Problem
sections.title: We knew the catalog. Our customers did not.
paragraphs: Mega menu choices, category structure, and shop-by paths were being debated internally without testing them against real users.
Navigation affects findability across the catalog. People who already know where products live are poorly placed to judge whether someone new can find them.

sections.label: The Journey
sections.title: Watch people use the front door.
paragraphs: I led moderated usability research into the navigation and information architecture. I used the findings to guide the redesign.
The study examined entry paths and the mega menu. It gave us evidence about the customer's mental model and the visibility of the navigation itself.
sections.decision: Use observed behavior to decide how the catalog should be entered.

sections.label: The Solution
sections.title: Start with the customer’s need
paragraphs: Moderated testing supported Shop by Condition as an entry point and exposed discoverability problems in the mega menu. I brought those findings into the navigation redesign.
The report gave the team a record of observed behavior and a format for later studies.
points: Customer needs as an entry point
Documented discoverability failures
A research report built for a design decision

sections.label: The Results
sections.title: Preference lost its monopoly.
paragraphs: The redesign had observed customer behavior to work from, and the team had a repeatable research-report format for its next study.

studies.title: A shared foundation for a second brand
studies.shortTitle: A shared foundation for a second brand
studies.summary: I defined the brand rules and documented the design foundation before the page count grew.
studies.scope: Theme tokens, brand layer, button variants, component evaluation
studies.collaboration: A documented foundation for the incoming designer and the shared commerce build.
atAGlance: A second brand needed a home on a platform without a design system.
Theme tokens and governance came before the pages.
I defined the design rules before the pages multiplied, giving the next designer a documented starting point.

sections.label: The Problem
sections.title: Every page could become another place to fix a brand.
paragraphs: A second brand needed to live inside an existing commerce platform. There was no design system.
Without a token layer, each new surface would need its own styles. A brand adjustment would become a search through pages and files, and every new page would add to that work.

sections.label: The Journey
sections.title: Decide what the pages should inherit
paragraphs: I defined color, typography, and spacing tokens, then layered the new brand over that base. I documented the button variants and their accessibility constraints.
I evaluated a component foundation and recorded the recommendation and reasoning so incoming work had explicit guidance.
sections.decision: Make the shared decisions once, before they spread across the interface.

sections.label: The Solution
sections.title: A brand layer on a shared foundation.
paragraphs: The theme separated brand choices from the underlying platform. Color, typography, spacing, and button variants had a documented foundation.
The incoming designer could build against that foundation on day one. Brand changes had a place to happen without a page-by-page styling pass.
points: Base tokens for shared decisions
A brand theme layered over the base
Accessibility flags in button tokens
A documented component recommendation

sections.label: The Results
sections.title: The brand had a foundation to maintain
paragraphs: The brand launched on the shared infrastructure. Brand adjustments could happen at the token layer, and the incoming designer had the decisions and their reasoning documented.

studies.title: Four documents, one checkout, zero agreement.
studies.summary: I used AI to compare conflicting requirements, made the experience decision, and recorded what engineering should build.
studies.scope: Checkout price presentation and requirements reconciliation
studies.collaboration: Engineering and product stakeholders working from conflicting written requirements.
studies.source: docs/case-studies-sanitized.md: Four Documents, One Checkout, Zero Agreement
atAGlance: Requirements disagreed on how to present a consult fee.
AI cross-referenced the sources; I made the experience decision.
I resolved conflicting price requirements and recorded which instructions the decision replaced.

sections.label: The Problem
sections.title: Both versions were written down. Both looked current.
paragraphs: Requirements documents called for an itemized consult fee at checkout. The latest meeting directive and the design called for one combined price. Engineering could build either, with a written source to justify it.
The conflict affected what a customer saw beside the Buy button. It needed an experience decision and a record of which requirements that decision replaced.

sections.label: The Journey
sections.title: Read the sources together, then make the call.
paragraphs: I used AI to cross-reference the requirements, meeting transcripts, and ticket history. Reading the records together exposed where the instructions disagreed.
I chose a combined price, matching a checkout pattern already converting with customers. AI identified the contradictions; the experience decision was mine.
sections.decision: Use a combined price, and record exactly which requirements it supersedes.

sections.label: The Solution
sections.title: Give engineering a decision that can survive the next meeting.
paragraphs: I documented the combined-price decision and tagged the superseded requirements with their sources. The record explained what changed and why.
Refund messaging remained an explicit dependency. It needed to match the combined-price model, otherwise resolving checkout would create another contradiction later in the experience.
points: A recorded combined-price decision
Source-linked superseded requirements
Refund messaging named as an open dependency

sections.label: The Results
sections.title: Engineering had a decision to build
paragraphs: I recorded the combined-price direction and the requirements it replaced. Engineering built against that record without another meeting cycle. Refund messaging remained an explicit dependency.
